<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
$\mu(\zeta(3))<5.5138800$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:rv}
If the sixteen integers above are positive and $c_0>c_2$, then
\[
  \mu(\zeta(3))\le\frac{c_0+c_1}{c_0-c_2}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
It would be natural to read the improvement as an increase of the arithmetic
saving. That is not what happens. Normalising by $52000$, so as to compare with
the Rhin--Viola direction, one finds
\[
\begin{array}{lcc}
 & \text{Rhin--Viola} & \text{here}\\
 c_0 & 47.154720796 & 47.155547848\\
 c_1 & 48.469409645 & 48.470066337\\
 \int d\psi \;(\text{saving}) & 24.187685304 & 24.186930081\\
 c_2 & 29.812314696 & 29.812839150
\end{array}
\]
The saving is in fact slightly \emph{smaller}, and $c_2$ slightly larger; the gain
comes from $c_0$ growing faster than $c_2$, by $8.3\cdot10^{-4}$ against
$5.2\cdot10^{-4}$ per unit. The cone is still the right mechanism, but it must be
read against the smooth behaviour of the saving at that distance, not against the
starting point.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Five such cones were found around the Rhin--Viola point, the best two giving
$-1.0653\cdot10^{-5}$ and $-1.0648\cdot10^{-5}$. This suggests that the
perturbative mechanism is close to exhausted here, and that a further improvement
would require a change of representation, as in \cite{Zu14} for $\zeta(2)$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is effective, like \eqref{eq:rv}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
